source.title: Finding and Reactivating Post-Trained LLMs' Hidden Safety Mechanisms
source.authors: Ming-Jie Li; Wai-Man Si; Michael Backes; Yang Zhang; Yi-Sen Wang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some prose and table formatting contain minor typographical or extraction irregularities, but the reported results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates harmful-response rates in post-trained reasoning and domain-specific models, and tests interventions to restore safety in those settings. It extends the broader safety-degradation topic, but does not test the specific mechanisms or interventions named in V1–V7.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-response evaluations and safety-restoration interventions in post-trained models. These results do not test the listed versions: the study does not compare fine-tuning on a few harmful or benign examples against an aligned starting checkpoint, measure per-token KL, test compliant-opening bypasses, identify a localized safety circuit, explain first-token shallowness, or test deepening safety across response positions. SafeReAct's few-layer adapters are a restoration method, not a test that safety is localized in those parameters. No labels are assigned.
record.test_reason: The paper takes safety loss after post-training as its premise and studies why it happens and how to restore safety. It reports harmful rates only for already post-trained models (R1-distilled, OpenThinker, UltraMedical, Finance-Llama). It never measures the aligned starting checkpoint under the same judge, so there is no before/after. It also says R1-distilled models were not trained from aligned LLMs. It measures nothing per token, tests no prefill or suffix attack, runs no harmful-example fine-tuning and tests no deepening. Neuron pruning targets reasoning neurons, not a safety-localization test. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that post-training masks, rather than removes, safety mechanisms through over-activated domain capabilities. Pruning those capabilities or applying SafeReAct restores safety while preserving task performance.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies post-trained reasoning and domain-specific models, neuron pruning, prompting, and representation alignment with LoRA adapters on selected layers. It does not use the original few-example harmful or benign fine-tuning recipe. SafeReAct is the proposed restoration method.
record.method_sensitivity: Safety outcomes vary across models, methods, and benchmarks. The authors report that Circuit-Breaker improves R1-8B but fails to improve safety consistently on the other models. SafeReAct's safety results are described as stable across tested α values on R1-7B and R1-8B, while reasoning performance varies with α. Safe suffixes and prompt methods also yield different safety rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning reasoning-associated neurons (Wanda set-difference) lowers harmful rates in R1-7B and R1-8B; random 20% pruning does not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In post-trained reasoning models, safety behaviour is masked by over-activated domain-capability neurons and returns when they are removed.

fits_no_version.finding: SafeReAct brings harmful rates to about 0–5% across four reasoning models while keeping GSM8K/MATH within about 3 points. Circuit-Breaker helps only R1-8B; SafeChain helps but leaves about 10% harmful and costs about 20 points of accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation alignment to a pruned-model safe representation restores refusal in post-trained LRMs more stably than Circuit-Breaker or SafeChain.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2025 (39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, as stated in the paper)
record.problems: The checklist says the experiments do not report error bars or statistical significance because reruns would require substantial time and computation. Figure 2 provides plotted values without numerical labels in the text. The paper's reported evaluations cover selected models and domains; its limitations state that models larger than 32B were not assessed.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, omitted Table 1 prompt-method harmful-rate results (Section 3.1), SafeReAct α ablation safety rates (Table 3), medical and finance safety results (Tables 4–5), benign-prompt rejection rates (Table 6), and larger-model results (Table 7). The Table 2 rows and Figure 2 rows were prioritized as the main cross-model safety outcomes and the neuron-pruning comparison. Also omitted reasoning-utility metrics because they are not harmful-response measures.

untested.parts: Post-training on reasoning, medical or finance data is assumed to erode safety. No aligned-base harmful rate is measured as a baseline, and R1-distilled models come from non-aligned bases.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefill, adversarial suffix or decoding attack; only safety-promoting suffixes and prompts.
Reasoning-neuron pruning and few-layer LoRA restore safety, but no test that safety lives in few weights.
The masking explanation concerns domain post-training, not why alignment is shallow across tokens.
No token-depth safety training or robustness evaluation of it.

missing.what: Prompt-based safety reactivation (ICD, PAT, Self-Remind) lowers harmful rates at a GSM8K cost; these are safety-promoting prompts, not bypasses.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with all versions not_tested and no labels is inconsistent; reclassified to assumes/T4. The main data issue is the Table 2 benchmark mislabelling, corrected via Table 1 and the prose. The paper itself notes R1-distilled models were not built on aligned LLMs, which weakens any V2 reading.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples, nor a before/after test of harmful-example fine-tuning.
No controlled before/after test showing ordinary or carefully chosen benign training data raises harmful compliance.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement or response-position analysis.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change bypass test. The safe suffixes and prompt methods studied are intended to improve safety.
The study prunes reasoning-associated neurons and trains adapters on selected layers; it does not establish that a small set of parameters carries safety behavior.
The paper proposes masking by post-trained capabilities as an explanation for safety degradation, but does not test why safety would be shallow across response tokens.
No training that spreads safety beyond early response tokens, or evaluation of its robustness, is tested.
